Triggers.value: A specific taste associated with the event

Maladaptive Strategies.value: control eating strictly to feel in control
try hard not think about the trauma

Threat.value: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it
My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank

Negative Appraisals.value: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it
I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me

issues.item: Triggers: Emotional Closeness: Someone getting emotionally close to me
issues.explanation: The trigger profile is dominated by interpersonal closeness plus taste and crying. For torture, gustatory and affective-expression triggers are plausible, but emotional closeness as a primary trigger is less well integrated with the rest of the profile, which contains no interpersonal betrayal/shame/relationship-based appraisals or memories to explain why closeness itself would be a salient cue. This creates a cross-node mismatch rather than a direct impossibility.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Gambling: I gamble to distract myself or feel excitement
issues.explanation: Gambling stands out as weakly connected to the rest of the formulation. The strongest active pathways involve triggers, negative appraisals, memory, and threat, but the other selected strategies are control/safety based (restrict eating, hypervigilance), whereas gambling is a sensation-seeking/distracting behavior with no support from the memory, threat, or appraisal items. It reads like a separate coping pattern rather than part of the same PTSD-maintaining loop.

'Concentration' is not a threat belief/state in the same way as the other threat items. 'Cannot Trust Safety' and 'Body Reacts Before Mind' reflect ongoing sense of current threat, but concentration difficulty is a nonspecific cognitive symptom and does not cohere tightly within the Threat node. Given the formulation emphasizes Memory → Threat and Maladaptive Strategies → Threat, a more direct threat-related item would be expected.

vignette: When Nalini was thirty-four, she was detained for fourteen months. Her captors kept her in a windowless room and, during the long interrogations, forced a thick, metallic-tasting broth down her throat to keep her conscious. The mixture was sharply bitter, laced with tamarind and crushed garlic, a flavor that clung to her tongue for days. She never expected to leave that room, yet she did. What followed was not a sudden recovery but a slow hardening of habits that made sense in the moment. Her body learned to brace for danger before her mind could register it, a physical flinch that arrived ahead of thought. She walked through her congregation with a steady, watchful posture, her eyes cataloging exits and reading posture for signs of threat. When others told her she was safe, the words simply slid off her; she could not bring herself to believe them. She tried hard not to think about what had happened, telling herself that if she let herself remember, she would not be able to handle it. Yet the memories surfaced anyway, arriving as fragmented pieces that refused to fit together. Sometimes, moments of the captivity struck her with terrifying precision—a boot heel scuffing concrete, the rustle of a nylon sleeve—while other stretches of those months remained entirely blank. When the fragments did surface, a wave of intense guilt followed, heavy and suffocating. Having navigated her divorce a few years prior, she had believed she could endure any isolation, but the weight of this silence eventually convinced her she was no longer capable of doing the things that had defined her, and a quiet hopelessness settled over her days, convincing her that nothing ahead would ever be different. Over the next two years, these experiences took root in her daily life as a pastor in suburban Ohio. The rigid control she once found in prayer became a strict regimen of eating. She began limiting her meals to plain rice, grilled chicken, and water, counting portions and chewing slowly, convinced that controlling what she consumed was the only way to keep the chaos contained. In the church, her avoidance grew into practical consequences. She stopped entering the pastoral office for one-on-one visits. When a parishioner once asked her to share how faith had sustained her through such darkness, Nalini sat with the woman until tears spilled over her lower lip, her throat closing around the memory of what had actually been done to her. She could not form words about the event, and the effort of speaking triggered an affect she could not suppress. She began leaving services early, citing fatigue. She spent her mornings scanning the fellowship hall for dangerous-looking individuals, her shoulders permanently tight, convinced that safety was an illusion. Her identity as a shepherd felt irreparably fractured; the voice that once comforted the grieving now trembled at the mere suggestion of vulnerability. The turning point came last month during a Wednesday sermon preparation. As she readied the text on resilience, her mind involuntarily turned to the interrogation room, and her body reacted to the imagined threat before she had even finished the first paragraph. She had to step into the vestry, pressing her palms against the cold sink until the shaking passed, realizing she could no longer sustain the distance she had built. She is finally sitting in this office because the weight of her silence has become heavier than the fear of remembering. What she hopes for is simply to reclaim the ability to stand at her pulpit without her hands trembling, to believe the word safety again, and to stop counting every crumb of her meals. What she fears most, however, is that if she opens the door to the past, she will shatter completely and will never be able to close it.
